macro.title: What It Means — VWRA, Bonds, Gold & BTC

reads.label: VWRA
reads.text: priced this week by the de-escalation relief and lower oil, not rates — hence record highs; the risk is a credibility-shy Fed and a firm long end reasserting once the oil relief is spent.

reads.label: Global bonds
reads.text: pinned near 52-week lows by the long-end selloff, so the equity–bond hedge works less well just as equities turn rich.

reads.label: Gold
reads.text: caught two ways — haven premium unwinding versus a softer dollar and a Fed-credibility hedge; net firmer near US$4,065.

reads.label: Bitcoin
reads.text: the tell — it did not join the record rally, slipping ~1.3% while stocks made highs, because tight liquidity prices it more than any Iran headline. Analysis of the moves, not a call.

stories.headline: The Deal Both Sides Say Isn't Happening
stories.dek: A week after Trump called off the weekend strikes and claimed the "perimeters" of a deal, the deal has un-happened. On Monday Tehran denied it is talking to Washington at all, US officials told CBS no new negotiations are planned, and the president — contradicting both — pivoted to demanding "Total Surrender." Oil, at least, took him at the softer word: Brent fell almost 5%.

stories.headline: Frontier Video, Open Weights, One Card
stories.dek: MiniMax dropped the weights of its H3 video model on Hugging Face this week, and ComfyUI merged native support the same day. It makes fifteen-second 2K clips with stereo sound in a single pass — and, at a 42-gigabyte footprint, it is the first frontier-class video generator that fits on a workstation instead of a cluster. The catch is in the licence, not the hardware.

stories.headline: Two Rival Nations Catch Mars Losing Its Air
stories.dek: A study out this week caught the solar wind whipping waves onto the very edge of Mars's atmosphere and flinging it to space — and confirming it took NASA's and China's spacecraft watching at once. It is a detection, like this fortnight's others, made by reading a trace rather than seeing the thing.

stories.headline: SG61 Comes Home to Kallang — Under a Red Sky Warning
stories.dek: Sunday's National Day Parade returns to the National Stadium for the first time in a decade, promising an indoor drone show and the biggest effects in NDP's history. Overhead, a forecast nobody controls: the region's haze outlook is on red for only the second time since 2019, with August and September named the danger months.

stories.headline: A Tender Closes on the Southern Waterfront — and Nobody Yet Knows the Bid
stories.dek: At noon today the state's first land parcel in the Greater Southern Waterfront closes for tender, and the analysts can't agree whether developers will show up. One house sees four bidders and a cautious price; another sees seven and pays up. The bids reveal at the close — a rare case where the guess is all we have.

stories.headline: A Bigger Battery, a Thinner Case, a Seven-Hundred-Dollar Ask
stories.dek: The Galaxy Watch Ultra 2 starts reaching wrists this week — 47mm of titanium, a screen that hits five thousand nits, and a battery a third larger than before. Reviewers call it Samsung's best watch yet. The awkward part: the endurance gain is smaller than the battery suggests, and the far cheaper Watch 9 does most of the same job.

stories.headline: One Dimmer for Every Awkward Load
stories.dek: Lutron's new LED+ Pro Max dimmers reach distributors and Home Depot's site this month — a single switch engineered to tame the whole messy list of modern LED loads without the flicker and the buzz. They are, pointedly, not smart. For a Lutron-plus-Home-Assistant house, that is exactly the point.

stories.headline: Japan Puts a Private Room Back on the Bullet Train
stories.dek: From October the Tokaido and Sanyo Shinkansen get "Supreme Class" private compartments — proper cabins with a door that shuts, the first of their kind on Japan's mainline bullet trains in a generation. Tickets open 15 September. And the yen, even after this week's rare rescue, is still soft enough to make the splurge sting less (p15).

stories.headline: The Biggest Weekend the Movies Have Ever Had
stories.dek: Two films did it together. "Spider-Man: Brand New Day" opened to a record-setting US$355 million while Nolan's "The Odyssey" refused to fade — and between them Hollywood posted its largest domestic weekend in history, US$429 million, past the 2019 "Endgame" frame. The receipts are real. Whether the numbers mean what the headlines say is the honest question.

stories.headline: The World's Toughest Phone Law Meets Its First Report Card
stories.dek: Australia banned under-16s from social media outright — the furthest any country has gone. Eight months in, the first hard data landed this week: teen usage fell barely four points, accounts fell ten, and half the children were never even asked to prove their age. The lesson isn't that the ban failed. It's exactly what a ban can and can't do.

stories.kicker: The Macro Desk · Rates & the Regime
stories.headline: Oil Crashes, Stocks Cheer — and the Bond Market Shrugs
stories.dek: The Iran de-escalation knocked almost 6% off crude in a day and lit a risk-on rally to fresh records — the S&P's first close above 7,600. But the long end of the bond market never flinched: the 30-year sits at a 2007 high, and the new Fed chair's credibility gap is untouched. Bitcoin, tellingly, sat the party out. Two clocks, running at different speeds.

stories.headline: Young People Still Want Families. They Say They Can't Afford Them.
stories.dek: The largest survey of its kind — 108,000 people across 73 countries — finds the barrier to the children young adults say they want isn't a change of heart. It's a bank balance: money, housing, job security. In the city with one of the world's lowest birth rates, that reads less like foreign news than a mirror.

stories.headline: It May Matter When You Train, Not Just How Much
stories.dek: A large ageing study finds that people whose activity is more rhythmic, regular and earlier in the day have higher aerobic fitness and move more efficiently — independent of how much they do in total. Treat it as an idea gaining traction, not a law. And the field's own scientists are quietly cooling the longevity hype the reader is sold daily.

stories.headline: The On-Sales to Set an Alarm For
stories.dek: National Day comes home to Kallang, the Grand Prix confirms a two-race weekend with its headliners named, and a rare August sky invites a dark-sky trip. Two on-sale dates below are worth a reminder — the booking, not the intention, is what gets you in.

stories.headline: The Planet at the Tip of a Pen
stories.dek: On a September night in 1846, an astronomer aimed his telescope at a patch of apparently empty sky and found a planet that had been discovered on paper first — deduced entirely from the wobble it left in another world's orbit. It is the founding story of a habit this whole issue runs on: when the thing itself won't show, read the trace it leaves.
